entries.q: I don't know what help I need. Where do I start?

entries.q: What do "income limit" and "Federal Poverty Level" mean?
a: An income limit is the most money your household can have coming in and still qualify for a program. Many programs set their limit as a percent of the Federal Poverty Level (FPL). The FPL is an income amount the federal government sets each year.

In 2026, 100% of the FPL is $15,960 a year for one person, $21,640 for two, $27,320 for three and $33,000 for four. Add $5,680 for each extra person. "200% of poverty" means double that amount. For example, 200% for a family of four is $66,000 a year, or $5,500 a month.

Gross income is your total income before taxes or anything else is taken out. Net income is what is left after the deductions a program allows. For example, SNAP (food stamps) checks gross income first, then net income after subtracting things like part of your earnings, child care, high rent and utility costs, and some medical bills for members who are 60 or older or disabled.

Who counts as your "household" depends on the program. For SNAP, it is the people who live together and buy and make meals together. Spouses and most children under 22 who live with you always count, even if they eat separately. For health coverage through NY State of Health, your household is usually you, your spouse and the people you claim as dependents on your taxes.
Each program has its own rules, so being a little over a chart does not always mean you are not eligible. The only sure way to know is to apply. Not sure where to start? Call 211.

entries.q: What papers should I bring when I apply for benefits?
a: Bring what you have, but do not wait to apply just because something is missing. For SNAP, the office must accept your application as long as it has your name, address and signature. If you qualify, benefits count from the day you applied.

Most offices ask for: a photo ID; Social Security numbers for each person applying (or proof you applied for one); proof of where you live, like a lease, rent receipt or mail; proof of income, like pay stubs from the last 4 weeks or a benefit award letter; your rent or mortgage bill and your heat, utility and phone bills; and bank statements. Also bring child care receipts, medical bills (for anyone 60 or older or disabled), and a doctor's statement if someone is disabled, unable to work or pregnant.

If you are not a U.S. citizen, bring your immigration papers. You can apply for your children or other eligible family members even if you are not applying for yourself. For SNAP, the office is not allowed to ask for immigration papers from people who are not applying.

If you are missing a paper, tell the worker. Other kinds of proof often work, like a statement from your landlord or employer. You will get a written notice listing anything still needed and the due date. When renewing SNAP, you get at least 10 days. Send copies, not originals. If your county uses the NYDocSubmit phone app, you can upload papers with it.
Warren County DSS posts a full checklist online (warrencountyny.gov/socserv/bring). Washington and Saratoga County DSS can tell you what they need when you call.

entries.q: What's the difference between DSS, OTDA, NY State of Health and Social Security?
a: Your county Department of Social Services (DSS) is where most people apply for and manage SNAP, cash assistance (Temporary Assistance), emergency help, HEAP and child care help. DSS also handles some Medicaid: people on SSI, people who need long-term care at home, the spend-down program, and some people with disabilities.

Local DSS offices: Warren County DSS, 1340 State Route 9, Lake George, 518-761-6300. Washington County DSS, Municipal Center, Building B, 383 Broadway, Fort Edward, 518-746-2300. Saratoga County DSS, 152 West High Street, Ballston Spa, 518-884-4140.

The Office of Temporary and Disability Assistance (OTDA) is the state agency that oversees DSS. You usually do not visit OTDA. It runs myBenefits.ny.gov, the OTDA Hotline (1-800-342-3009), fair hearings when you disagree with DSS, and the state child support program. It also helps decide Social Security disability claims for New Yorkers.

NY State of Health is the state's official health plan marketplace. Most people under 65 apply there for Medicaid, the Essential Plan, Child Health Plus or a private plan. Many people 65 and older or on Medicare who do not need long-term care now get Medicaid through it too. Call 1-855-355-5777. If you start in the wrong place, staff will help you get to the right one.

Social Security is a federal agency, separate from the state and county. It handles Social Security retirement, SSDI, SSI and Medicare sign-up. Call 1-800-772-1213 or find your nearest office at ssa.gov/locator. Not sure who to call? Dial 211.

entries.q: What is Medicaid, and how do I apply in New York?
a: Medicaid is public health coverage for certain people with low income, including children, families, pregnant people, older adults, and people with disabilities. It pays for a wide range of care. Some services have small co-pays; the state says these can be waived if you cannot afford them.

Most people apply through NY State of Health, online or by calling (855) 355-5777. This includes adults 19 to 64 without Medicare, children, pregnant people, and parents or caretaker relatives. New York is also moving more people there: people who have both Medicare and Medicaid, people 65 and older who are not asking for long-term care, and people applying for a Medicare Savings Program.

Some people still apply through their county Department of Social Services (DSS). This includes people who get SSI, people who are blind or disabled and do not fit the groups above, people who need long-term care at home (such as personal care or CDPAP), and people using the spend-down (excess income) program. If you start in the wrong place, staff will help you get to the right one.
Questions? Call the New York State Medicaid Helpline at (800) 541-2831.

entries.q: What is "straight" (fee-for-service) Medicaid?
a: "Straight" Medicaid, also called fee-for-service, means you are not in a Medicaid health plan. You show your Medicaid card at any doctor, dentist or other provider who is enrolled in New York Medicaid, and Medicaid pays that provider directly.

Some people cannot join a plan, so they stay on straight Medicaid. This includes people on spend-down (excess income), people who have other full health insurance, and people in hospice when they enroll. Some others, such as American Indians and Alaska Natives, may choose not to join a plan.
Even people in a Medicaid plan get some services straight from Medicaid instead of the plan. These are called "carve-outs." That is one reason to keep your Medicaid card after you join a plan.

Not every provider takes straight Medicaid. Ask the office, "Do you take straight (fee-for-service) Medicaid?" New York also publishes a public list of providers enrolled in Medicaid. In this directory, look for the "Straight Medicaid (fee-for-service)" tag.

entries.q: What is a Medicaid managed care plan, and how do I switch plans?
a: Most people with Medicaid must join a Medicaid managed care plan, which is a health plan approved by the state. You do not lose your Medicaid benefits; you get them through the plan.

In a plan, you pick a regular doctor, called a primary care provider (PCP), who helps coordinate your care and refers you to specialists. You usually must use doctors and hospitals in the plan's network. The plan pays those providers directly.

After you join a plan, you have 90 days to change your mind and switch. After those 90 days, you must stay in the plan for the next nine months, unless you have an urgent reason. Each family member can be in a different plan.
To learn about plans, switch, or ask about an exemption, call New York Medicaid Choice at 1-800-505-5678 (TTY 1-888-329-1541). It is the state's managed care enrollment program.

entries.q: What Medicaid changes are coming in 2026 and 2027?
a: A 2025 federal law (H.R. 1) is changing some Medicaid rules in New York.

Starting October 1, 2026, some immigrants (such as refugees, asylees, parolees, and survivors of domestic violence or trafficking) may move from Medicaid to the Essential Plan. Their benefits are not supposed to change. Coverage for children and pregnant people is not changing.

Starting January 1, 2027, some adults ages 19 to 64 will need to show they work, go to school, are in job training, or volunteer. They can meet the rule by earning at least $580 a month or doing 80 hours a month of these activities. Many people are excused, including people 65 or older, people who are pregnant, people with a disability, people with Medicare, and parents or caregivers of a child under 14.
Also starting January 1, 2027, some adults 19 to 64 will need to renew Medicaid every 6 months, and Medicaid will not pay for past medical bills as far back as it does now.
What to do now: make sure NY State of Health or your county Department of Social Services has your current address, phone and email, and open every notice you get.

entries.q: What is a Medicaid spend-down (excess income)?
a: If your monthly income is a little over the Medicaid limit, you may still get Medicaid through the Excess Income program, also called "spend-down" or "surplus income." The amount your income is over the limit works like a deductible.
It is for people who are under 21, 65 or older, certified blind or disabled, pregnant, or the parent of a child under 21.

Each month, once your medical bills (paid or unpaid) add up to your excess income amount, Medicaid pays your other covered bills for the rest of that month. If you have no bills, you can choose to pay your excess amount to the county instead (the "Pay-In" option).

Bills for you, your spouse, or your children under 21 can count. Old unpaid medical bills you still owe can also count. Ask your county Department of Social Services to start, and send bills early in the month.

entries.q: What is Health Home care management?
a: A Health Home is not a building. It is a group of health and service providers that work together for you. Once you enroll, you get a care manager who works with you on a care plan.
A care manager can help connect you to doctors, mental health and substance use care, medicines, housing, and services like food, benefits and transportation.

To qualify, you must have Medicaid and either two or more chronic conditions (such as asthma or diabetes) or one of these: HIV/AIDS, serious mental illness (adults), sickle cell disease, or serious emotional disturbance or complex trauma (children). A substance use disorder alone does not qualify, but it counts as one of two conditions.
To enroll, ask your Medicaid plan, doctor, hospital, discharge planner, or county Department of Social Services, or contact a Health Home directly.

entries.q: Can Medicaid give me a ride to a medical appointment?
a: Yes. Medicaid members can get free non-emergency rides to and from medical appointments, such as the doctor or the dentist. Rides are not given to pharmacies, gyms, schools or grocery stores. For an emergency, call 911.
In Warren, Washington and Saratoga Counties, rides are arranged by Medical Answering Services (MAS). Call the upstate line at (866) 932-7740 or set up an account on the MAS website.
Call at least 72 hours (3 days) before your appointment. Every trip must be approved ahead of time.
The ride type depends on your needs. It can be a bus, taxi, ambulette, or money back for mileage if you or someone you know drives you.

entries.q: What is Managed Long Term Care (MLTC)?
a: Managed Long Term Care is for people with Medicaid who are chronically ill or disabled and want to stay at home. A long-term care plan covers services like home health aides, personal care, nursing at home, therapy at home, adult day health care, and CDPAP.
There are three kinds: MLTC partial capitation plans (age 18 and up), Medicaid Advantage Plus plans (age 18 and up), and PACE (age 55 and up).

To join, you must be assessed as needing these services for more than 120 days. You must also meet the state's "minimum needs" rule: needing at least limited hands-on help with more than two daily activities (like bathing or dressing), or, with dementia or Alzheimer's, needing supervision with more than one.
The assessment is done by the New York Independent Assessor Program (see the NYIA question). Then New York Medicaid Choice helps you pick a plan.

entries.q: What is CDPAP, and can a family member be paid to care for me?
a: CDPAP (Consumer Directed Personal Assistance Program) is a Medicaid program that lets people who qualify for home care choose and hire their own caregiver, called a personal assistant.
The assistant can be a friend or family member, but not your spouse, your designated representative, or (for someone under 21) a parent.

To qualify, you need an assessment showing you need home care. Adults 21 and older must also meet the minimum needs rule that started September 1, 2025. You must be able to direct your own care, or have a designated representative who can.
Since 2025, every CDPAP member must use one statewide company, Public Partnership LLC (PPL), to handle the assistant's payroll.

sections.title: Health insurance words and medical bills

entries.q: What do insurance words like premium, deductible, copay and coinsurance mean?
a: A premium is what you pay each month to have insurance, even if you never see a doctor. A deductible is the amount you pay for covered care each year before your plan starts to pay its share.

A copay (copayment) is a set dollar amount you pay for a visit or a prescription, like $25. Coinsurance is a percent of the bill you pay after you meet your deductible. For example, with 20% coinsurance you pay $20 of a $100 visit, and the plan pays $80.

The out-of-pocket maximum is the most you have to pay for covered care in a plan year. After you reach it, the plan pays the full cost of covered care for the rest of the year. Your monthly premiums do not count toward it.

A network is the group of doctors, hospitals and other providers your plan has a contract with. In-network care costs you less. Out-of-network care usually costs more, and some plans do not pay for it at all except in an emergency (see the question on surprise bills).

Prior authorization means your plan must approve a service or medicine before it will pay. A referral is a written order from your main doctor to see a specialist; many plans require one. Before a big test or a specialist visit, call the number on your insurance card and ask: Is this provider in my network? Do I need a referral or prior authorization?

entries.q: How do I keep my Medicaid? What happens at renewal?
a: Medicaid does not continue forever on its own. You must renew it (also called recertifying) to keep it. Most people renew once a year. Starting in 2027, most adults ages 19 to 64 will renew every 6 months instead. If you apply before January 1, 2027, or renew before March 1, 2027, you get 12 months first (see the question on Medicaid changes).

If you signed up through NY State of Health, the state first tries to renew you on its own, using information it already has. You may not need to do anything. If it needs more, it will send you a notice asking you to log in to your NY State of Health account and send information. To find your renewal date, log in at nystateofhealth.ny.gov and click the "Plans" tab.

If your Medicaid is handled by your county Department of Social Services (DSS), for example if you get SSI, are on spend-down, or get long-term care at home, your county handles your renewal. Watch your mail and call your county DSS with questions. More people with Medicare and people 65 and older are being moved to NY State of Health.

Open every letter, text and email from NY State of Health, your county or your health plan, and answer by the date it gives. The state sends a warning at least 15 days before coverage ends. Keep your address, phone and email up to date so notices reach you.

If your Medicaid ends because you did not send in information, you have 90 days to send it and be reviewed without starting a new application. If you think Medicaid was ended by mistake, you can ask for a fair hearing (see that question). For help, call NY State of Health at 1-855-355-5777 (TTY 1-800-662-1220), call the Medicaid Helpline at 1-800-541-2831, or meet with a free enrollment assistor.

entries.q: I can't pay my hospital bill. Can I get help?
a: Yes. Every New York hospital licensed by the Department of Health must offer financial assistance (sometimes called charity care). All of them must use the same form, the NYS Uniform Hospital Financial Assistance Application. Ask the hospital's billing or financial aid office for it.

You may qualify if you have no insurance, if your insurance benefits have run out, or if you have insurance but paid more than 10% of your income on medical costs in the last 12 months. People with household income up to 400% of the federal poverty level are eligible. Below 200%, the hospital must waive all charges; between 200% and 400%, it must give a large discount. Only income counts, not your house, car or savings. Immigration status does not matter.

You can apply at any time, even after the bill goes to collections. You do not have to pay while your application is being decided. Payment plans can't be more than 5% of your monthly income, and interest is capped at 2%. A hospital can't refuse needed care because of an unpaid bill, and it can't sue patients under 400% of the poverty level. This law covers hospital bills, not separate bills from doctors who are not hospital employees.

New York also protects people with medical debt. Hospitals and health care providers can't put a lien on your main home or garnish your wages for medical debt, and medical debt is not allowed on your credit report. Be careful: if you pay a medical bill with a regular credit card, it is no longer medical debt and you lose these protections. A provider can't require you to keep a credit card on file before you get needed care.

For free help applying or appealing a denial, call Community Health Advocates at 1-888-614-5400. To report a hospital or provider breaking these rules, call the Attorney General's helpline at 1-800-771-7755 or email HFAL@health.ny.gov.

entries.q: I got a surprise bill from a doctor or hospital outside my network. What can I do?
a: A surprise bill is a bill from an out-of-network provider that you did not choose, often after emergency care or a hospital stay. Both federal law (the No Surprises Act) and New York law protect you.

For emergency care, and for care from an out-of-network doctor at an in-network hospital or surgery center, you usually only have to pay what you would pay in-network: your normal copay, coinsurance or deductible. Air ambulance bills are also protected under federal law. Billing you for more than that (called balance billing) is not allowed.

In New York, it can also be a surprise bill if your in-network doctor sent you to an out-of-network provider or lab and you did not sign a paper saying you knew they were out-of-network. For this kind of bill, you must send a Surprise Medical Bill Certification Form to your health plan and the provider. The form is on the NY Department of Financial Services (DFS) website.

If you have no insurance or are paying for care yourself, providers must give you a Good Faith Estimate of the cost before scheduled care. If your bill is at least $400 more than the estimate, you can dispute it, within 120 days of getting the bill.

What to do: don't ignore the bill, but don't pay the extra amount yet. Call your health plan and the provider and say you believe it is a surprise bill. For help, call DFS at 1-800-342-3736 or the federal No Surprises Help Desk at 1-800-985-3059 (open 7 days a week).

entries.q: Does Medicaid cover dentures, glasses and hearing aids?
a: Yes. New York Medicaid covers medically necessary dental, eye and hearing care, both with straight Medicaid and in Medicaid health plans. You must use a provider who takes Medicaid. Some items need prior approval (permission from Medicaid first); your provider asks for it for you.

Teeth: Medicaid covers exams, cleanings, X-rays, fillings, pulling teeth, root canals, crowns and dentures. Implants, including a single implant, can be covered when your dentist shows they are medically necessary and other choices like dentures won't work. Dentures, even if lost or broken, are usually replaced only once every 8 years, unless your dentist shows a new set is medically necessary.

Eyes: Medicaid covers eye exams and glasses, usually one exam for glasses and new lenses every two years. You can get them sooner for some conditions, like diabetes, glaucoma, a fast-changing cataract, or a child's quickly changing eyesight. Lost or broken glasses can be replaced. Contact lenses are covered only when medically necessary.

Hearing: With a referral from a doctor, physician assistant or nurse practitioner, Medicaid covers hearing tests. It also covers hearing aids, ear molds, batteries and repairs when testing shows you need them. Adults 21 and older need prior approval for two hearing aids. A lost, stolen or broken hearing aid can be replaced if it is out of warranty. Medicaid does not pay for FM systems, listening devices or tinnitus maskers.

Small copays may apply. A Medicaid dentist can't charge you more than the copay unless you agree and sign a private-pay agreement before treatment starts. To find a provider who takes Medicaid, call your health plan or the Medicaid Helpline at 1-800-541-2831, or search this directory for "Straight Medicaid".

entries.q: Can I see a doctor if I don't have insurance?
a: Yes. Community health centers, also called Federally Qualified Health Centers (FQHCs), are clinics that get federal funding and must serve everyone, even people who can't pay. They offer medical, dental, mental health and substance use care. Many have on-site pharmacies with discounted medicines, and some can help with rides.
Health centers adjust what you pay based on your income and family size. This is called a sliding fee scale. It can also help people who have insurance but can't afford their deductible or copays.

In this area, Hudson Headwaters Health Network is an FQHC with many health centers. Its Sliding Fee Program lowers the cost of medical and dental care, X-rays and many prescriptions. You can apply whether or not you have insurance. Ask at any Hudson Headwaters health center or call its Sliding Fee Program at (518) 824-8640.

To find other health centers, use the federal Find a Health Center tool at findahealthcenter.hrsa.gov. Also check whether you qualify for free or low-cost coverage like Medicaid or the Essential Plan (see those questions), and ask any hospital about financial assistance.

entries.q: My pharmacy says my medicine isn't covered. What can I do?
a: A generic drug has the same active ingredient as the brand-name drug and works the same way, but usually costs less. A formulary (drug list) is the list of medicines a plan covers. Some drugs need prior authorization, which means your prescriber must get the plan's OK first.

If you have Medicaid, your medicines are covered by NYRx, New York's Medicaid drug program. Since April 1, 2023, this includes people in most Medicaid health plans. People in long-term care plans (like MLTC, MAP or PACE) and the Essential Plan get drugs through their plan instead. Most pharmacies in New York take NYRx.

NYRx copays are $1 for generics and preferred brands, $3 for non-preferred brands, and 50 cents for over-the-counter medicine. There is no copay for people under 21, during pregnancy, or for mental health medicines and birth control, among others. A pharmacy can't refuse to give you your medicine because you can't pay the copay.

If the pharmacy says a drug isn't covered, ask why. Often it needs prior authorization, or a "preferred" drug on the list would work. Ask your doctor to request approval from Medicaid or switch you to a preferred drug. If the pharmacist can't reach your doctor, the pharmacist can get approval to give you up to a 72-hour emergency supply. Questions: Medicaid Helpline, 1-800-541-2831.

If you have a Medicare drug plan (Part D), you or your doctor can ask the plan for a "coverage determination" or an "exception." Your doctor must explain why you need that drug. If the plan says no, you can appeal. For help with drug costs, see the questions on Extra Help and EPIC.

entries.q: Can immigrants get Medicaid or the Essential Plan in New York?
a: It depends on immigration status, age, income, and whether you are pregnant. Some rules changed in 2026 because of a federal law (H.R. 1). Apply or ask before you decide you can't get coverage.

Children under 19 can get Child Health Plus no matter their immigration status, if they otherwise qualify. Pregnant people can get full Medicaid no matter their immigration status, with coverage for 12 months after the pregnancy ends. NY State of Health says coverage for children, pregnant people and people who recently gave birth is not changing.

Starting October 1, 2026, some immigrants, including refugees, asylees, parolees, and survivors of domestic violence or human trafficking, may move from Medicaid to the Essential Plan. Their benefits are not supposed to change. Since July 1, 2026, DACA recipients with income over 138% of the poverty level no longer qualify for the Essential Plan. Some lawfully present immigrants who get tax credits may see cost changes starting in 2027.

Undocumented adults ages 19 to 64 can usually get only Emergency Medicaid, if they meet the income rules. Emergency Medicaid pays to treat an emergency medical condition, including labor and delivery. Undocumented adults 65 and older may qualify for full Medicaid in New York, which started in 2024 and is paid with state funds.

To apply, call NY State of Health at 1-855-355-5777 or meet with a free enrollment assistor. Not sure where to apply? Call the Medicaid Helpline at 1-800-541-2831. If you are worried about your immigration case, see the question on public charge. A free legal aid office can help with your situation.

entries.q: Will using Medicaid or other benefits hurt my green card application ("public charge")?
a: Public charge is a test immigration officers use when some people apply for a green card (permanent residence). Officers look at your age, health, family, money and skills to decide if you are likely to depend on the government in the future.

The rules changed on September 18, 2026. Officers may now consider most income-based benefits, such as Medicaid, SNAP or housing help, that you apply for or get on or after that date. Getting a benefit does not by itself mean you will be denied; it is one part of the whole picture. Benefits you got before September 18, 2026 are judged under the older rule, which only counted cash assistance and long-term care in an institution paid by the government.

Many people are not affected. The test is part of a green card application, not a citizenship application, and it usually does not apply to people who already have a green card. Refugees, asylees, people applying for TPS, VAWA self-petitioners, T and U visa holders, and special immigrant juveniles are exempt.
Benefits your family members get, like a U.S. citizen child's Medicaid, are not counted as your own benefits. But officers may look at your whole household's money situation.

These rules are new and could change. Before you drop or turn down health coverage or food help, get advice. Call the New York State Office for New Americans hotline at 1-800-566-7636 (free, anonymous, many languages) to be connected with free immigration legal help.

entries.q: Can I get VA health care as a veteran?
a: You may be eligible for VA health care if you served in the active military, naval or air service and did not get a dishonorable discharge.

VA has expanded care to veterans exposed to toxins or other hazards, including those who served in the Vietnam War, Gulf War, Iraq, Afghanistan, or any combat zone after 9/11.

entries.q: Who can get Medicare, and when does it start?
a: Medicare is federal health insurance for people 65 or older who meet citizenship or residency rules. Some people under 65 can get it earlier because of a disability, End-Stage Renal Disease (ESRD, permanent kidney failure), or ALS (Lou Gehrig's disease).

Age 65: if you already get Social Security retirement or disability benefits before you turn 65, you usually get Medicare automatically. If not, you sign up through Social Security. Part A usually starts the month you turn 65.

Disability: Social Security automatically enrolls you in Medicare Parts A and B after you have received disability benefits (SSDI) for 2 years. With ALS, Medicare generally starts the first month you are eligible for disability benefits.

ESRD: Medicare usually starts on the first day of the fourth month of dialysis, at any age, if you meet the work history rules. It can start sooner if you do home dialysis training or get a kidney transplant.
SSI by itself does not qualify you for Medicare.

entries.q: What are Medicare Parts A, B, C and D?
a: Part A (hospital insurance) helps cover hospital stays, skilled nursing facility care, hospice, and some home health care.

Part B (medical insurance) helps cover doctors and other providers, medical equipment like wheelchairs and walkers, and many preventive services like screenings and shots. Part B has a monthly premium.

Part C is Medicare Advantage: a private plan approved by Medicare that bundles Parts A and B, and usually D. You may need to use the plan's network and get approval before some care. Many plans add extras like vision, hearing and dental.
Part D helps pay for prescription drugs. You get it from a private drug plan added to Original Medicare, or through a Medicare Advantage plan that includes drug coverage.
Original Medicare is Parts A and B. Medigap is extra insurance you can buy to help pay what Original Medicare does not, like the 20% coinsurance.

entries.q: When can I sign up for Medicare or change my Medicare plan?
a: Initial Enrollment Period: 7 months around your 65th birthday. It starts 3 months before the month you turn 65 and ends 3 months after it. Signing up late can mean a lifelong late penalty.

General Enrollment Period: January 1 to March 31 each year, if you missed your first chance. Coverage starts the month after you sign up. A Special Enrollment Period may let you sign up later without a penalty, for example within 8 months after job-based coverage ends.
Open Enrollment: October 15 to December 7 each year. You can join, switch or drop a Medicare Advantage or drug plan. Changes start January 1.
Medicare Advantage Open Enrollment: January 1 to March 31. If you are already in a Medicare Advantage plan, you can switch plans or go back to Original Medicare.
If you have Medicaid or get Extra Help, you may be able to change your drug coverage once a month.

entries.q: What is a Medicare Savings Program (QMB, SLMB, QI)?
a: A Medicare Savings Program (MSP) uses Medicaid to help people with limited income pay Medicare costs. Every MSP pays the Part B premium, so it is no longer taken out of your Social Security check.

In New York there are two main levels. QMB (Qualified Medicare Beneficiary) also pays Part A premiums if you have them, plus Medicare deductibles and coinsurance. With QMB, Medicare providers are not allowed to bill you for Medicare cost-sharing. QI (Qualifying Individual) pays the Part B premium only.

For 2026 in New York, QMB is for incomes at or below $1,836 a month for one person ($2,489 for a couple). QI is for incomes below $2,474 a month ($3,355 for a couple). These limits change each year; check the current limits on the state's MSP page.
New York has no resource (savings) test for MSP. When you get an MSP, you also automatically get Extra Help with drug costs.

You may see "SLMB" on federal websites; New York's own MSP page lists QMB and QI. To apply, mail form DOH-4328 to your county Department of Social Services, or apply with NY State of Health. Questions: Medicaid Helpline, (800) 541-2831.

entries.q: What is Extra Help (the Part D Low-Income Subsidy)?
a: Extra Help is a Medicare program that helps people with limited income and resources pay for Medicare drug coverage (Part D): premiums, deductibles and co-pays. While you have it, you also do not pay a Part D late penalty.

You get Extra Help automatically if you have a Medicare Savings Program or get SSI. Otherwise, you can apply through Social Security, and a free State Health Insurance Assistance Program counselor can help.

If you have Medicaid or get Extra Help, you may be able to change your drug plan once a month.

entries.q: Should I choose Medicare Advantage or Original Medicare with a Medigap plan?
a: With Original Medicare (Parts A and B), you can see any doctor or hospital in the U.S. that takes Medicare, usually without referrals or prior approval. But you pay 20% coinsurance for most services, with no yearly limit. Many people add a Medigap policy (Medicare Supplement Insurance) to help pay those costs, plus a separate Part D plan for drugs.

Medicare Advantage (Part C) is a private plan that you use instead of Original Medicare. Most include drug coverage, and many add extras like some dental, vision or hearing care. Each plan has a yearly limit on what you pay. But you usually must use the plan's network, and you may need referrals and prior approval for some care. You can't use a Medigap policy with Medicare Advantage.

The trade-off in short: Medicare Advantage puts everything in one plan with a yearly cost limit, but gives you less choice of doctors and more approvals. Original Medicare plus Medigap gives you more choice and fewer approvals, but you pay a premium for the Medigap policy and the drug plan on top of Part B.

New York gives you extra protection. If you have Parts A and B, you can buy a Medigap policy at any time of year, and the company can't turn you down or charge more because of your health or age. This includes people under 65 who have Medicare because of a disability. A policy can make you wait up to 6 months for coverage of a health problem you already had, but that wait is shortened if you had other coverage with no gap of more than 63 days.

You can change Medicare plans from October 15 to December 7 each year, with changes starting January 1. If you are in Medicare Advantage, you can also switch plans or go back to Original Medicare from January 1 to March 31. Before you decide, call HIICAP at 1-800-701-0501 or your county Office for the Aging for free counseling (see the question on help choosing a Medicare plan).

entries.q: What is hospital "observation status," and why does it matter for rehab in a nursing home?
a: In the hospital, you are either an inpatient or an outpatient. You are an inpatient only after a doctor writes an order to admit you. If you are "under observation," you are an outpatient, even if you stay overnight in a regular hospital bed.

This affects what you pay. As an outpatient, you usually pay a copay for each hospital service under Part B, and the pills you normally take at home may not be covered. It matters even more if you need rehab afterward. Original Medicare pays for a skilled nursing facility only after an inpatient stay of at least 3 days in a row. Time under observation or in the emergency room does not count.

If you are under observation for more than 24 hours, the hospital must give you a Medicare Outpatient Observation Notice (MOON). It tells you that you are an outpatient and why. Ask your doctor, "Am I an inpatient or under observation?" If you may need rehab, ask whether you should be admitted.

If you were admitted as an inpatient and the hospital later changed you to observation, you may have the right to a fast appeal. This right started February 14, 2025, for people in Original Medicare. You should get a Medicare Change of Status Notice before you leave; if you don't, ask for it. Appeal to the Quality Improvement Organization (BFCC-QIO) named on the notice, ideally while you are still in the hospital.
Medicare Advantage plans may have different rules, and some waive the 3-day stay. For help, call 1-800-MEDICARE (1-800-633-4227), or see the question on free help choosing a Medicare plan (HIICAP).

entries.q: I have both Medicare and Medicaid. Which one pays, and what plans can I join?
a: People with both Medicare and Medicaid are called "dual eligible." Medicare pays first for Medicare-covered care. Medicaid pays after that, and covers things Medicare doesn't, like long-term care at home or in a nursing home. Medicaid may also pay your Medicare premiums, deductibles and coinsurance (see the Medicare Savings Program question).
Your prescriptions are covered by a Medicare drug plan (Part D), not by Medicaid. You automatically get Extra Help with drug costs.

You can keep Original Medicare and straight Medicaid, or join a plan that puts both together. New York has three kinds of these integrated plans. Medicaid Advantage Plus (MAP) is for adults 18 and older who need long-term care for more than 120 days. PACE is for people 55 and older who need long-term care, with a care team and a day center. IB-Dual is for people who don't need long-term care: you keep your Medicaid health plan and join the same company's Medicare plan for dual eligibles, called a D-SNP.

If you are in a Medicaid health plan when you become eligible for Medicare, your plan may sign you up for its D-SNP automatically. It must send you a notice at least 60 days before. You can say no by calling your plan. In these plans you usually must use the plan's doctors.

Free help choosing: HIICAP at 1-800-701-0501, New York Medicaid Choice at 1-888-401-6582 (for MAP), or Medicare at 1-800-633-4227. If you have a problem with a plan, ICAN (the Independent Consumer Advocacy Network) gives free help at 1-844-614-8800.

entries.q: What is the difference between SSI, SSDI and Social Security retirement?
a: SSI (Supplemental Security Income) is for people who are 65 or older, blind, or disabled AND have very little income and resources. It does not depend on your work history. In New York, people who get SSI generally also get Medicaid.

SSDI (Social Security Disability Insurance) is for people with a disability who have worked and paid Social Security taxes long enough, generally 5 of the last 10 years. The amount depends on your past earnings. After 2 years on SSDI, you get Medicare.
Social Security retirement can start as early as age 62 if you worked and paid Social Security taxes for 10 years or more. Medicare is separate and generally starts at 65.
Many people get both SSI and Social Security benefits. It is possible to have both Medicare and Medicaid. If you have SSI and Medicare, you automatically get Extra Help with drug costs.
To apply or ask questions, call Social Security at 1-800-772-1213 (TTY 1-800-325-0778).

entries.q: Who can get SSI, and how much does it pay?
a: SSI pays monthly benefits to adults and children who are blind, have a disability, or are 65 or older, and who have little or no income and resources.
Resources are things you own, like money in the bank. The limit is $2,000 for one person or $3,000 for a couple. Your home, one car used for transportation, and household goods do not count.

For 2026, the most the federal government pays is $994 a month for one person and $1,491 for an eligible couple. Other income lowers the payment. New York adds a State Supplement (SSP) for most SSI recipients, and people eligible for SSP automatically get Medicaid.
There is no online SSI application in New York; call Social Security at 1-800-772-1213 to make an appointment. You must report changes in income, resources and living situation every month.

entries.q: How does SSDI work, and how long is the wait?
a: SSDI pays monthly benefits to people with a disability or blindness that will keep them from working for a year or more, or is expected to result in death, and who have enough work history.
If you are working, your earnings must be below a limit called "substantial gainful activity." In 2026, that is $1,690 a month ($2,830 if you are blind).
There is a 5-month waiting period. Benefits generally start in the sixth full month after the date Social Security decides your disability began. There is no waiting period for ALS.
Medicare starts automatically after you have received SSDI for 2 years (sooner for ALS). Part A is free; Part B has a monthly premium.
You may be able to go back to work, or keep working, without losing your SSDI benefits. Ask Social Security about the work rules before you start a job, and report any work.

entries.q: When can I start Social Security retirement benefits?
a: You can start retirement benefits as early as age 62 if you worked and paid Social Security taxes for 10 years or more.

If you start before your full retirement age, your monthly check is reduced a little for each month you start early. For people born in 1960 or later, full retirement age is 67, and starting at 62 lowers the check by about 30%.
If you wait past full retirement age, up to age 70, your monthly benefit goes up.
Medicare is separate. Most people sign up for Medicare Parts A and B when they are first eligible, usually at age 65.

entries.q: What is a representative payee?
a: A representative payee is a person or organization that Social Security picks to receive and manage Social Security or SSI payments for someone who cannot manage their own money.

entries.q: What is an ABLE account?
a: An ABLE account is a tax-advantaged savings account for a person with a disability. The money can pay for disability-related costs like housing, transportation, health care and education.

Starting January 1, 2026, the disability must have begun before age 46 (it used to be age 26). People on SSI or SSDI because of a disability that started before 46 can qualify, and others can qualify with a signed disability certification.
For SSI, the first $100,000 in an ABLE account does not count toward the $2,000 resource limit. Medicaid continues even if the ABLE balance goes over that.
Anyone can put money in. The yearly contribution limit is $20,000 in 2026, and a person can have only one ABLE account.

entries.q: Can I work while I get SSI or SSDI?
a: Yes. Social Security has "work incentives," rules that let you try working without losing all your benefits at once. Always report your work and your pay to Social Security.

SSI: Social Security does not count $20 of your income and the first $65 you earn each month, and it counts only half of your earnings above that. So your SSI check goes down about $1 for every $2 you earn. Students under 22 can have up to $2,410 a month of earnings not counted (up to $9,730 in 2026). Some costs you pay because of your disability so you can work can also be subtracted. If your check stops because of your pay, you can often keep Medicaid, and SSI can restart without a new application if your pay drops.

SSDI: you get a Trial Work Period of 9 months (within a rolling 5 years) when you keep your full check no matter how much you earn. In 2026, any month you earn over $1,210 counts as a trial month. After that comes a 36-month period when you get your check for any month you earn less than "substantial gainful activity" (SGA). In 2026, SGA is $1,690 a month, or $2,830 if you are blind.

If your benefits stop because of work and your condition later keeps you from working, you can ask for Expedited Reinstatement within 5 years. You can get up to 6 months of temporary payments while Social Security decides.

Free help: Ticket to Work offers free job services to people 18 to 64 on SSI or SSDI. Free benefits counseling (WIPA) explains how a job will affect your benefits before you take it. Call the Ticket to Work Help Line at 1-866-968-7842 (TTY 1-866-833-2967). Also ask your county DSS about New York's Medicaid Buy-In for working people with disabilities.

entries.q: I got a Social Security overpayment letter. What can I do?
a: An overpayment means Social Security says it paid you more than it should have. The letter says why and how much. Read it right away, because the first 30 days matter.

If you think the amount is wrong, or that you were not overpaid at all, file an appeal called a "reconsideration." You have 60 days after you get the letter. If you appeal within 30 days, Social Security will not collect until it decides.

If the amount is right but it was not your fault and you cannot afford to pay it back (or it would be unfair), ask for a waiver. Use form SSA-632. You can upload it through your my Social Security account, or mail or fax it to your local office. If you ask within 30 days, Social Security will not collect until it decides.

If you do nothing, Social Security will start keeping 50% of your monthly Social Security benefit, or 10% of your SSI payment, until it is paid back. To pay less each month, send form SSA-634. To pay or set up a payment plan, call 1-855-807-8807, Monday to Friday, 8 a.m. to 4:30 p.m. If you no longer get benefits, the money can be taken from tax refunds or wages.
A free legal aid office can help with your situation. You can also call Social Security at 1-800-772-1213 (TTY 1-800-325-0778). Keep copies of everything you send.

entries.q: How can I save money and still keep SSI or Medicaid?
a: SSI has a resource limit: $2,000 for one person or $3,000 for a couple. Resources are things like cash, bank accounts, stocks and savings bonds. If what you own is over the limit at the start of a month, you get no SSI for that month.

Many things do not count: your home, household goods, one car used for transportation, burial spaces, up to $1,500 each in burial funds for you and your spouse, and life insurance with a total face value of $1,500 or less. Back payments from SSI or Social Security do not count for 9 months. Tax refunds, including the EITC, do not count for 12 months.
An ABLE account lets some people with disabilities save up to $100,000 without it counting for SSI. See "What is an ABLE account?" for who qualifies.

Trusts: a supplemental (special) needs trust for a disabled person under 65, or a pooled trust run by a nonprofit for a disabled person of any age, does not count for SSI or Medicaid if it is set up correctly. When the person dies, money left over pays Medicaid back. Money the trust pays to you directly counts as income. For SSI, trust payments for rent or housing can lower your check (by up to $351.33 a month in 2026), but payments for things like phone bills or medical care do not.

Pooled trusts and spend-down: in New York, a person who is certified disabled can put their extra (excess) income into a pooled trust each month. Medicaid then does not count that income, which can end the monthly spend-down. The trust pays the person's bills, such as rent and utilities, from that money. Give your county DSS a copy of the trust and a written statement of how much you will deposit each month. Talk to a lawyer before setting up any trust; a free legal aid office can help with your situation.

entries.q: What tax credits can put money in my pocket, even if I don't owe taxes?
a: Some tax credits are "refundable." That means if the credit is more than the tax you owe, you get the rest back as a refund. You must file a tax return to get them, even if you don't owe any taxes.

The federal Earned Income Tax Credit (EITC) is for people who work and earn low to moderate pay. For tax year 2025 (the returns filed in 2026), it is worth up to $649 with no children, $4,328 with one child, $7,152 with two, and $8,046 with three or more. Income limits depend on family size. For example, a single parent with one child could earn up to $50,434. New York State has its own earned income credit that adds to the federal one.

The federal Child Tax Credit is worth up to $2,200 for each child under 17 for tax year 2025. Up to $1,700 per child can come back as a refund if you earned at least $2,500. You (and your spouse, if filing jointly) and each child need a Social Security number that is valid for work.

New York's Empire State Child Credit is also refundable. It is for full-year New York residents with a child under 17. For tax year 2025, it is up to $1,000 for each child under 4 and $330 for each child age 4 to 16. For tax year 2026 (filed in 2027), the amount for ages 4 to 16 goes up to $500. See the next question for free help filing.

entries.q: How do I get unemployment benefits in New York?
a: Unemployment Insurance (UI) pays weekly benefits to people who lost their job or had their hours cut, and who are ready, willing and able to work. You need enough recent wages from work. For claims in 2026, the state calculator looks for at least $3,500 in wages in at least one calendar quarter (a 3-month period). If you quit or were fired, apply anyway. The Department of Labor (DOL) will review your claim.

File in your first week out of work, because waiting can cost you benefits. Apply online at unemployment.labor.ny.gov (best between 7:30 a.m. and 7:30 p.m.). Or call the Telephone Claim Center at 1-888-209-8124, Monday to Friday, 8 a.m. to 5 p.m. Interpreters are available by phone. The first payment usually comes 2 to 3 weeks after your claim is processed.

How much and how long: your weekly amount is based on your past wages. The most anyone can get is $869 a week. You can get up to 26 weeks of benefits. To estimate your amount, use the DOL Benefit Rate Calculator.

"Certifying" means asking for each week's payment. You must do it every week you are out of work. Weeks run Monday to Sunday. Certify for the past week any time from that Sunday through the next Saturday, online or by phone at 1-888-581-5812. Report any work you did, even if it was only an hour. You must also do at least 3 work search activities each week, or follow an official work search plan.
If you are denied, you have 30 days from the date of the decision to ask for a hearing. Note: DOL is upgrading its unemployment system starting November 2, 2026, which may delay some payments.

entries.q: How do I get or change child support in New York?
a: Your county's child support office can help you get a support order from Family Court. Once there is an order, the Support Collection Unit collects payments from the other parent, keeps track of them, and sends them to you.

To start, enroll online at childsupport.ny.gov. Or fill out a Child Support Enrollment Form and a Family Safety Screening Form and give them to your local child support office. If you apply for cash assistance, you are referred automatically, and Medicaid applicants may be too. If working on child support would go against your child's best interests, for example because of safety, tell the worker. You can refuse without penalty.

Family Court figures support using a set guideline: a percent of the parents' income after certain deductions (17% for one child, 25% for two, 29% for three, 31% for four and at least 35% for five or more), plus each parent's share of child care, medical and school costs. A $35 yearly fee applies only to parents who never got cash assistance and who receive more than $550 in support in a year.

Changing an order: only a court can change it, so keep paying the full amount until it does. Either parent can ask Family Court for a change (Form 4-11) if there is a big change in circumstances. For orders from October 13, 2010 or later, you can also ask if 3 years have passed, if either parent's gross income changed by 15% or more, or if you are in jail or prison. Every 2 years the program also checks orders for a cost-of-living increase.
Questions? Call the Child Support Helpline at 888-208-4485 (TTY 866-875-9975), Monday to Friday, 8 a.m. to 7 p.m. A free legal aid office can help with your situation.

entries.q: What is SNAP (food stamps), and what are the work rules?
a: SNAP gives monthly benefits on an EBT card to buy food at approved stores. It helps low-income working people, older adults, people with disabilities and others. Eligibility depends on household size, income and other factors, and most households do not have a savings (resource) test.

Starting October 1, 2026, the most a household can get is $306 a month for one person and $1,023 for four people. Most households get less. Apply at myBenefits.ny.gov or at your county Department of Social Services. OTDA Hotline: 1-800-342-3009.

Work rules: adults 18 to 64 who are able to work and do not live with a child under 14 (called ABAWDs) can get SNAP for only 3 months in 3 years, unless they work, train or volunteer at least 80 hours a month. Many people are excused, for example people 65 or older, households with a child under 14, people who get disability benefits, and people who cannot work 80 hours a month because of a physical or mental health reason.

If you lost SNAP between June 1 and September 30, 2026 because of these work rules, the time limit reset on October 1, 2026 and you can reapply. Call your county DSS if you think you should be excused.
Tip: you can freeze your EBT card when you are not using it to help protect your benefits from theft.

entries.q: What is Temporary Assistance (cash assistance), and what about emergencies?
a: Temporary Assistance (TA), also called Public Assistance, is cash help for people who cannot work, cannot find a job, or do not earn enough. It is run by your county Department of Social Services.

Family Assistance is for families with a minor child living with a parent or caretaker relative. Adults have a lifetime limit of 60 months. Safety Net Assistance is for people who do not qualify for Family Assistance; cash Safety Net is generally limited to 2 years in a lifetime, and after that help comes in non-cash form, such as payments made directly to a landlord or utility.

Emergency Assistance can help with an urgent need, like an eviction notice, a utility shut-off notice, no heating fuel in cold weather, or violence or threats from a partner or household member. You do not need to be on ongoing TA to get emergency help.
If you have an emergency, contact your county DSS as soon as possible. You should be interviewed and told the decision in writing the same day you apply.

entries.q: What is HEAP (help with heating bills)?

entries.q: What is the difference between LIHEAP, HEAP and weatherization?
a: LIHEAP is the federal program that funds help with home energy costs. It does not give grants directly to people, and it never charges a fee for a benefit. To get help with heating bills in New York, apply for HEAP (see the HEAP question).

entries.q: What can I do if DSS denies or cuts my benefits? (Fair hearings)

entries.q: How do SNAP interviews and renewals work, and what if my EBT benefits are stolen?
a: After you apply for SNAP, you must do an eligibility interview, by phone or in person. You should get a decision within 30 days. If you have little or no money, ask to be checked for "expedited" (fast) SNAP. If you qualify, you get your first benefits within 7 days.

Renewing (recertification): about two months before your benefits end, you get a packet in the mail with a form and a phone interview time. Send in the form before the interview date, at myBenefits.ny.gov or by mail, fax or in person. You can also ask for a face-to-face interview. If your form arrives after the interview date, it is up to you to reschedule before your benefits end.

Reporting changes: your notice tells you what to report. Under New York's usual rules, you must report if your household's total monthly income before taxes goes over the limit on your notice. Report it within 10 days after the end of that month. If you are approved for more than 6 months, you also get a Periodic Report form halfway through. Return it within 10 days. If you don't report, you may have to pay benefits back.

Stolen benefits: thieves can copy EBT cards with hidden "skimmers" on card readers, or trick you with fake texts and calls. Stolen SNAP benefits can no longer be replaced. Stolen cash assistance (TA) may be replaced once a year if you apply within 30 days of finding the theft. Either way, call EBT Customer Service at 1-888-328-6399 right away for a new card.

Protect your card: use the ebtEDGE app or ebtEDGE.com to freeze your card between uses, change your PIN often, and block out-of-state and online purchases. Never give your PIN to anyone who calls or texts you.

entries.q: Can my power or heat be shut off? What protections do I have in New York?
a: New York's Home Energy Fair Practices Act (HEFPA) protects people with electric or gas service at home. Before a shutoff, your utility must send a written final notice and wait 15 days so you can pay or make a payment plan. Shutoffs can only happen Monday to Thursday, 8 a.m. to 4 p.m. They are not allowed on holidays, the day before a holiday, or the two weeks around Christmas and New Year's. You have a right to pay overdue bills in reasonable installments based on what you can afford (a "deferred payment agreement").

Medical emergency: if someone in your home has a serious illness or condition that a shutoff would make worse, get a certificate from a doctor or the local board of health. Your service may not be shut off while it is in effect. After 30 days the doctor must renew it, and you must show you cannot pay. If the service runs life-support equipment, the certificate stays in effect, but every 3 months you must show why you cannot pay.

Older, blind or disabled: tell your utility if you are 62 or older, blind or disabled, and everyone else at home is 62 or older, 18 or younger, blind or disabled. The utility must then make special efforts to reach you before and after a shutoff. From November 1 to April 15, utilities must also make a special effort to find out if turning off heat would seriously harm anyone's health or safety.

Energy Affordability Program (EAP): large electric and gas utilities give a monthly bill discount to lower-income customers. You may be signed up automatically if you get HEAP, SNAP, Medicaid, SSI or some other benefits. If you think you qualify but don't see the discount, call your utility.

If you get a shutoff notice, call your utility first to set up a payment plan. If that doesn't work, call the Department of Public Service emergency hotline at 1-800-342-3355 (business days, 7:30 a.m. to 7:30 p.m.). For other utility complaints, call 1-800-342-3377. Also ask your county DSS about Emergency HEAP and emergency assistance.

entries.q: Is there help paying for a funeral or burial?

entries.q: What is the difference between Section 8 and public housing, and how do waiting lists work?
a: A Section 8 Housing Choice Voucher helps pay rent in a private apartment or house that you find. The housing agency pays part of the rent straight to the landlord. You usually pay about 30% of your adjusted monthly income, and up to 40% in some cases. You can sometimes move with your voucher.
Public housing is apartments or homes owned and run by a local housing authority. Your rent is usually based on 30% of your adjusted income, with a small minimum rent.

Both are for low-income households, including older adults and people with disabilities. You apply with your local housing agency. Demand is high, so you will usually go on a waiting list, and some lists close. For vouchers, you can apply to more than one waiting list, and you do not have to live in that area to apply.

For Warren, Washington and Saratoga Counties, New York State Homes and Community Renewal (HCR) lists JEM Inc. in Saratoga Springs, (518) 372-8846, as its local Section 8 administrator. You can apply online for open HCR waiting lists through the MyHousing Portal, or on paper with the local administrator.
While you wait, keep the housing agency up to date on your address, phone and household size, or you may be removed from the list.

entries.q: What does "homeless" mean for housing programs (HUD categories)?
a: HUD-funded homeless programs use four categories.

Category 1, literally homeless: sleeping in a place not meant for people to live (like a car or outside), staying in a shelter or transitional housing, or leaving an institution (like a hospital or jail) after 90 days or less, if you were homeless right before you went in.
Category 2, imminent risk: you will lose your home within 14 days and have no other place or resources to get housing.

Category 3 covers some people who count as homeless under other federal laws. Category 4 covers people fleeing or trying to flee domestic violence, dating violence, sexual assault, stalking or human trafficking, who have no other safe place to live.
Which category you are in can affect which programs you qualify for. Tell the worker exactly where you slept last night and how long you have been there.

entries.q: How does an eviction work in New York, and what should I do at each step?
a: In New York, a landlord must go to court to evict you. Only a sheriff, marshal or constable can remove you, and only with a court order called a warrant of eviction. Changing the locks, shutting off your electric or water, taking your things, or keeping you out without that order is an illegal eviction, and it is a crime. If it happens, call the police, then call a free legal aid office.

In a case about unpaid rent, the landlord should first send a late notice by certified mail if rent is more than 5 days late. Then the landlord must give you a written 14-day rent demand. If you do not pay within those 14 days, the landlord can start a court case. The court papers (a notice of petition and a petition) must be delivered 10 to 17 days before the court date. If the landlord just wants to end or not renew your tenancy, the landlord must give you 30, 60 or 90 days' written notice, depending on how long you have lived there.

Do not ignore court papers. If you do not go to court, you can lose the case without being heard. At your first court date, you can ask for time to get a lawyer, and the judge must postpone the case for at least 14 days. Bring your lease, rent receipts, letters, and photos of any repair problems. Problems like needed repairs can be a defense.

If the landlord wins, the judge signs a warrant of eviction. A sheriff, marshal or constable must then give you a notice with 14 days to leave, and evictions happen only on business days. In a case about unpaid rent, paying everything you owe before the eviction is carried out stops it. If you get a 14-day notice, act right away. The only way to stop or delay it is a written request to the court, called an order to show cause.

Get free help as early as you can. Outside New York City, apply online through EvictionDefenderNY on LawHelpNY, or call the Legal Aid Society of Northeastern New York at (833) 628-0087. For help paying back rent, ask your county Department of Social Services (DSS) about emergency assistance, or call 211. A free legal aid office can help with your situation.

entries.q: What are my basic rights as a renter in New York (deposits, repairs, Section 8)?
a: Security deposit: a landlord cannot ask for more than one month's rent as a deposit, and cannot ask for last month's rent on top of it. After you move out, the landlord has 14 days to return the deposit, or to give you an itemized list of what was taken out for damage. If the landlord does not send that list within 14 days, they must return the whole deposit. You can ask the landlord to inspect before you move out, so you have a chance to fix problems. (Rent-regulated apartments have different deposit rules.)

Other money rules: before you sign a lease, the most a landlord can charge for a credit and background check is $20, and they must give you a copy. Rent is not late until it is more than 5 days past due, and a late fee can be no more than $50 or 5% of the monthly rent, whichever is less.

Repairs: every lease includes a promise that your home will be livable, safe and clean. This is called the "warranty of habitability." Examples of problems are no heat or hot water, or bugs that are not taken care of. Tell the landlord in writing, keep a copy, and take photos. You can also report problems to your local housing or code enforcement office. Be careful about holding back rent: the landlord can sue you for it, although a judge may lower the rent if the landlord did not make repairs. It is illegal for a landlord to punish you for a good-faith complaint.

Section 8 and other income: in New York, a landlord cannot refuse to rent to you, or treat you differently, because you pay with a Section 8 voucher, public assistance, Social Security, child support or any other lawful source of income. This is called source-of-income discrimination.

To report discrimination, contact the NYS Division of Human Rights at (844) 697-3471 or use its online form. It is free and you do not need a lawyer. You generally have 3 years from the discrimination to report it. For security deposit problems, call the NY Attorney General's office at 1-800-771-7755.

entries.q: How do I ask my landlord for a change because of a disability?
a: If you have a disability, federal and New York law say a housing provider must make reasonable changes so you can use and enjoy your home. A "reasonable accommodation" is a change to a rule, policy or service. A "reasonable modification" is a physical change to your home or a shared area.

Examples of accommodations: an assigned parking space near your door when parking is usually first-come; an assistance animal in a "no pets" building; letting a friend mail your rent if your disability makes it hard to leave home; or, in a voucher program, extra time to find a unit or an extra bedroom for a live-in aide. The landlord cannot charge you an extra fee or deposit for an accommodation.

Examples of modifications: grab bars in the bathroom, a ramp at the entrance, wider doorways, or lever door handles. In most private housing, the landlord must allow the change but you pay for it, and you may have to put the inside of the unit back when you move out. In public housing and other federally funded housing, the housing provider usually pays, unless the cost would be an undue burden.

How to ask: you can ask out loud, but it is best to ask in writing and keep a copy. Say that you have a disability, what change you need, and how it helps. If your disability is not obvious, the landlord may ask for reliable proof that you have a disability and need the change. A letter from a doctor or other medical professional, a peer support group, a service agency, or another reliable third party can work.

If you are turned down, ask why, and whether another change would meet your need. You can file a free complaint with the NYS Division of Human Rights at (844) 697-3471. A free legal aid office can help with your situation.

entries.q: I have nowhere to sleep tonight. What do I do?
a: Contact your county Department of Social Services (DSS) as soon as you can. If you are homeless, DSS can give emergency help, including paying for a shelter or a motel stay. You do not have to already get Temporary Assistance (cash assistance) to get emergency help. DSS should interview you and tell you its decision in writing the same day you apply.

After business hours, on weekends and on holidays, each county keeps an emergency number for DSS. Some counties have it answered by the sheriff's office or another emergency center. Check the DSS listing for your county in this directory for the after-hours number, or call 211.

In winter, New York has "Code Blue" rules. When the temperature, with wind chill, is expected to drop below 32 degrees for at least 2 hours, the county must call a Code Blue and take emergency steps to get people who are homeless out of the cold. A Code Blue lasts until it warms above 32 degrees, and at least until 7 a.m. the next morning. Our directory lists local Code Blue shelters.

211 Northeast NY covers Warren, Washington and Saratoga Counties. Dial 2-1-1, or (888) 366-3211, to find shelter and other help. If you are in danger, call 911. If you are fleeing abuse, call a 24-hour domestic violence hotline (in the crisis bar at the top of this site). They can help you get to a safe place, and they keep shelter locations private for safety.

entries.q: How do I get an order of protection, and what if it is broken?
a: An order of protection is a court order that tells someone to stop hurting, threatening or harassing you. A judge can order the person to stay away from you and your children, to move out, to give up guns, or not to harm pets. A New York order is good anywhere in the state, and it can be enforced in other states too.

Family Court is for people who are "family or household members": a current or former spouse, someone you have a child with, a relative by blood or marriage, or someone you have or had an intimate relationship with, even if you never lived together. You file a family offense petition at your county's Family Court. It is free to file. You have the right to a lawyer in Family Court, and the court will assign one if you cannot afford one.

Criminal court can give an order of protection when the person has been charged with a crime, for example after an arrest. The district attorney asks the judge for it. Family Court is your own case; in criminal court the police or district attorney bring the charges.

Family Court may give you a temporary order the same day you ask. It usually lasts until the next court date. If Family Court is closed, a local town or city court can give a temporary order, and then you go to Family Court when it opens. An order only works after it has been served (formally delivered) to the other person. A final Family Court order can last 1 to 5 years.

If the person breaks the order, call 911. Breaking an order of protection is a crime. You can also file a violation petition in Family Court. Keep a copy of your order with you; you can also ask for a free wallet-size Hope Card that police will enforce. For help any time, call the NYS Domestic and Sexual Violence Hotline at 1-800-942-6906, or text 844-997-2121.

entries.q: I am being abused at home. What is a safety plan, and what other protections are there?
a: A safety plan is your own plan to stay safer and be ready if you are in danger. It can include a code word to tell friends you need help, copies of important papers kept where you can get them, a bag packed with clothes, money and medicine for you and your children, a safe place to go, and ways to protect your phone and internet use. A domestic violence advocate can help you make one. If you are in danger now, call 911.

You can call the NYS Domestic and Sexual Violence Hotline any time at 1-800-942-6906, or text 844-997-2121. Warren and Washington Counties and Saratoga County also have 24-hour local hotlines, listed in the crisis bar at the top of this site. These programs can help you find a safe place to stay. For safety, we never list where shelters are.

New York's Address Confidentiality Program (ACP) is free. It gives you a substitute mailing address in Albany to use instead of your real address, and forwards your mail to you. It is for victims of domestic violence, sexual offenses, human trafficking, stalking and kidnapping who have moved or are moving for safety. People in your household can join too. An application assistant, often at a domestic violence program, can help you apply. ACP phone: (855) 350-4595.

Ending a lease early: under New York law (Real Property Law 227-c), if you or someone in your household is a victim of domestic violence and fears more violence by staying, you can end your lease. Give the landlord written notice at least 30 days before you plan to leave. Within 25 days of the notice, give proof, such as an order of protection or a police report. The landlord must keep this private.
The Legal Aid Society of Northeastern New York has a domestic violence program for Warren, Washington and Saratoga Counties: call (833) 628-0087. A free legal aid office can help with your situation.

entries.q: Can I get help paying costs after I was the victim of a crime?
a: Yes, you may. The NYS Office of Victim Services (OVS) can pay back some out-of-pocket costs caused by a crime that happened in New York. This is called crime victim compensation. Not every victim qualifies for every kind of help. OVS pays last, after other sources like health insurance or workers' compensation.

OVS can help with: medical and counseling costs; lost wages or lost support, up to $30,000; funeral and burial, up to $12,000; moving and storage, up to $2,500; repairing or replacing essential personal property, up to $2,500; crime scene cleanup, up to $2,500; rides to crime-related medical appointments and court; and domestic violence shelter costs.

Rules changed on December 31, 2025. You now have 3 years to file a claim, and OVS can accept a late claim for a good reason, such as not knowing the program existed. Instead of a police report, you can tell a local victim service provider, or a medical or mental health professional, and they can send OVS a short form. OVS can decide your claim even if no one was arrested or convicted.

To apply, use OVS Compass online or a paper application from ovs.ny.gov. You do not need a lawyer or a Social Security number. A local victim assistance program can help you apply for free. Call OVS at 1-800-247-8035, Monday to Friday, 8 a.m. to 5 p.m.

entries.q: How do I get a free lawyer for a problem that isn't a criminal case?
a: Civil legal aid is free help from a lawyer for problems that are not criminal charges. Legal aid offices often help with eviction and housing, homelessness prevention and foreclosure, public benefits like SNAP or disability, family matters like orders of protection, problems for older adults, and some consumer and tax problems.

Free legal aid is mostly for people with low income. The Legal Aid Society of Northeastern New York (LASNNY) says your household income should generally be at or below 200% of the federal poverty level (about twice the poverty line). Some of its projects have higher income limits or none at all.

In Warren, Washington and Saratoga Counties, LASNNY has an office in Saratoga Springs. Call (833) 628-0087 toll-free or (518) 587-5188 (Relay 711). Intake by phone goes on each day until the schedule fills, so call early. If LASNNY can't take your case, it may refer you for free to a volunteer private lawyer for some problems, such as divorce, bankruptcy, wills and consumer debt.

LawHelpNY.org has a free directory of legal help by county, plain-language guides and forms, and a LiveHelp chat (Monday to Thursday, 9 a.m. to 9 p.m.). If you are facing eviction outside New York City, apply through EvictionDefenderNY on LawHelpNY.

entries.q: What is the difference between guardianship, a power of attorney and a health care proxy?
a: All three let someone else make decisions for a person. The big differences are who picks the helper, what decisions they cover, and whether a court is involved.

A power of attorney (POA) is a paper you sign to name an "agent" to handle your money and property, like banking, bills, benefits and taxes. You choose the agent. It does not cover medical decisions. You must be at least 18 and able to understand what you are signing, and it must be notarized. A health care proxy is a separate form that names someone to make medical decisions only if you cannot. Many people need both. (See our entry on health care proxies and MOLST.)

Guardianship is when a judge appoints someone to make decisions for a person who can no longer manage. It takes a court case, and the judge may pick someone the person would not have chosen. A POA and health care proxy only work if they are signed while the person can still understand them. Planning ahead can often avoid guardianship.

New York has two kinds of adult guardianship. Article 81 (Mental Hygiene Law) can be used for any adult who cannot manage personal needs or property. The court looks at what the person can and cannot do, not just a diagnosis. A court evaluator looks into the case, there is a hearing, and the judge gives the guardian only the powers that are needed. It is meant to be a last resort.

Article 17-A (Surrogate's Court Procedure Act) is for adults with an intellectual or developmental disability. It is filed in Surrogate's Court and often gives the guardian full powers. Supported decision-making, where a person picks trusted helpers but keeps their own rights, is a less restrictive choice. A free legal aid office can help with your situation.

entries.q: What is Clean Slate, and will my old criminal record be sealed?
a: Clean Slate is a New York law that seals many old criminal convictions automatically, so you do not have to apply. It took effect November 16, 2024. The court system has up to 3 years from that date, until November 2027, to set up the process and seal records that already qualify. So many eligible records are not sealed yet.

A misdemeanor can be sealed 3 years after sentencing, or after release if you were in jail. A felony can be sealed 8 years after sentencing or release from prison. You must have no new convictions, no pending charges, and be off probation or parole. A new conviction, or having probation or parole revoked, restarts the clock. Sex offenses that require registration, murder and other non-drug Class A felonies are not sealed.

Sealed records are hidden from most background checks for jobs and housing. You do not have to list a sealed conviction on most NYS license applications, but until a conviction is actually sealed, you must still report it when asked. Police, courts and prosecutors can still see sealed records. So can some other checks, such as fingerprint background checks required by law, jobs with children, older adults or other vulnerable people, gun licenses, commercial driver's licenses and public housing.

To see your NYS record, ask the Division of Criminal Justice Services (DCJS) for a Record Review. You get fingerprinted through IdentoGo, (877) 472-6915. The fee is $17.50 for New York residents (as of February 2026), and you can ask for a fee waiver. Until the courts finish Clean Slate sealing, your record will still show convictions that will be sealed later. A free legal aid office can tell you if you can ask a court to seal a record sooner.
