entries.q: How do I replace a lost birth certificate or Social Security card?
a: Birth certificate: if you were born in New York State outside New York City, you can order a certified copy from the NYS Department of Health (DOH) Vital Records, or from the local registrar where you were born. The local registrar is usually the city, town or village clerk. If you were born in New York City, order from the NYC Health Department instead.

You can order your own birth certificate, or your child's if your name is on it. Others need a court order. DOH charges $45 online or by phone (plus a vendor fee), or $30 by mail. DOH says it has long delays right now. Local registrars also give copies; call ahead for their fee, hours and what to bring. DOH Vital Records: (855) 322-1022.

You need a copy of photo ID, such as a driver's license, NYS non-driver ID, passport or U.S. military ID. If you do not have photo ID, DOH accepts two papers that show your name and address, such as a utility or phone bill, or a letter from a government agency dated in the last six months.

Social Security card: a replacement is free. Often you do not need the card at all, just the number. Start online at ssa.gov; you may be able to finish there. If not, you will need an appointment at a Social Security office. The office cannot print a card for you; it comes in the mail 5 to 10 business days after your request is finished. Call 1-800-772-1213 (TTY 1-800-325-0778) for help.

entries.q: A debt collector is calling, or I got sued over a debt. What are my rights?
a: A debt collector must give you written "validation" information in its first message or within 5 days. It must name who you owe, break down the amount (interest, fees, payments and credits), and give a date by which you can dispute the debt, about 30 days. If you dispute in writing by that date, the collector must stop collecting the disputed amount until it sends proof.

Old debts: in New York, a collector generally has 3 years to sue you over consumer credit debt, like a credit card or loan. After that, they cannot sue you or threaten to sue. Making a payment after the 3 years are up does not restart the clock.

Some income is protected ("exempt") from debt collectors, including Social Security, SSI, public assistance, veterans' benefits, unemployment, workers' compensation, child support and pensions. If federal benefits like Social Security or SSI are directly deposited, your bank must leave you two months' worth even if a collector tries to freeze your account. If your account is frozen, tell the bank, the court and the collector in writing that the money is exempt, and get legal help right away. LawHelpNY lists the current protected amounts.

If you are sued, do not ignore the court papers. Respond by the deadline on the papers. Answering does not mean you admit you owe; it makes the collector prove the debt. If you do not answer, the court can give the collector a "default judgment." Then the collector may be able to take part of your pay (garnish wages) or freeze your bank account, and a judgment is hard to undo.

For free help, call the Legal Aid Society of Northeastern New York at (833) 628-0087. To complain about a debt collector, call the NY Attorney General at 1-800-771-7755. A free legal aid office can help with your situation.

entries.q: Should I call 988, 911, or a mobile crisis team?
a: Call 911 if someone is in physical danger right now. Examples are a suicide attempt in progress, a suspected overdose, or a medical emergency like chest pain or trouble breathing. 911 sends police, an ambulance or fire crews.

Call or text 988, the 988 Suicide & Crisis Lifeline, for a mental health, suicide or substance use crisis when no one is in immediate physical danger. You can also chat at 988lifeline.org. It is free, confidential and open 24 hours a day, 7 days a week. You can reach out for yourself or for someone you are worried about.

When you call 988, a recording first offers choices: press 1 for the Veterans Crisis Line, press 2 for Spanish, or stay on the line for a local crisis center. A trained counselor answers, asks if you are safe, listens, and shares resources. Most calls are handled on the phone. Counselors contact 911 only in a small share of calls, when a life is at risk, and usually with the caller's agreement.

A mobile crisis team is a small team of trained staff, often including a peer (someone with lived experience), who come to you: at home, at school, or another place in the community. It is voluntary and aims to help without police or a hospital stay when possible. In Warren, Washington and Saratoga Counties, Northern Rivers Family of Services runs mobile crisis teams for adults, children and teens. Find the number in the Crisis Help category of this directory. If the team is not available, call 988, or 911 in an emergency.

entries.q: What happens at a psychiatric emergency room, and what are my rights?
a: In a mental health crisis, a hospital emergency room doctor will examine you and decide what care you need. Some larger hospitals have a CPEP (Comprehensive Psychiatric Emergency Program), a 24-hour crisis center inside the hospital. A CPEP can keep someone in an observation bed for up to 72 hours, which often avoids a longer hospital stay.

Voluntary care means you agree to it. You sign a form asking to be admitted. If you want to leave, tell the hospital in writing. The hospital must then let you go promptly, unless the director thinks you need to stay. In that case, the hospital has 72 hours to ask a court for an order to keep you.

Involuntary care (sometimes called a hold) happens without your agreement. Under New York's Mental Hygiene Law, it is allowed only when a mental illness is likely to cause serious harm. That means a danger to yourself, a danger to others, or being unable to meet your own basic needs like food, shelter or medical care. Staff must try voluntary care first. In an emergency admission, a psychiatrist must confirm the need within 48 hours, and the stay can last up to 15 days. Keeping someone longer takes more doctor reviews, and you or someone acting for you can ask for a court hearing.

You have rights. You must get a written notice of your legal status and rights. You can have visitors, contact people outside the hospital, talk with a lawyer, and help make your treatment plan. Mental Hygiene Legal Service (MHLS) is a free, independent court agency. MHLS can answer your or your family's legal questions and represent you in court. Ask any staff member to connect you.

Family and friends can help. A patient age 16 or older can ask a relative or close friend to take part in treatment planning. The hospital must help plan care for after discharge. For insurance problems, the state's CHAMP help line is 888-614-5400. This is general information, not legal advice. For your situation, contact MHLS or a free legal aid office.

entries.q: Where can I get free Narcan (naloxone), and will I get in trouble for calling 911 during an overdose?
a: Naloxone (brand name Narcan) is a medicine that can reverse an opioid overdose. Opioids include heroin, fentanyl and many prescription pain pills. Signs of an overdose: the person can't be woken up, is breathing very slowly or not at all, makes gurgling sounds, or has blue or gray lips. Call 911 right away.

Ways to get naloxone in New York: Any pharmacy can give it to you without a prescription from your own doctor, through a statewide standing order. If you have insurance with drug coverage, the state's N-CAP program covers the copay, so you pay little or nothing. Registered community overdose prevention programs give free naloxone kits and free training. OASAS (the state Office of Addiction Services and Supports) also mails free naloxone through an online order form.

Fentanyl test strips check a drug for fentanyl, a very strong opioid that is often mixed into other drugs. You can order them free through the same OASAS form or get them from a local overdose prevention program.

New York's 911 Good Samaritan Law protects people of any age who call 911 for an overdose, and the person who overdosed. You can't be charged for having drugs (less than 8 ounces), having marijuana, having drug equipment, sharing drugs, or underage drinking. It does not protect against selling drugs, open warrants, or probation or parole violations. Questions: call 1-800-692-8528.

entries.q: How do I start medicine for opioid addiction (buprenorphine, methadone or naltrexone)?
a: Medicine is the standard treatment for opioid use disorder (opioid addiction). There are three medicines: buprenorphine (often called Suboxone or "bupe"), methadone, and a monthly naltrexone shot (Vivitrol). Buprenorphine eases withdrawal and cravings, and it helps protect against overdose if someone uses opioids again.

Buprenorphine can be prescribed in many places, including a regular doctor's office or clinic, and filled at a local pharmacy. The special "X-waiver" that prescribers used to need was removed by federal law at the end of 2022. Now any prescriber with a standard DEA registration for these medicines can prescribe it, and there is no limit on how many patients they treat.

Methadone for addiction can only be given at a certified opioid treatment program (OTP), sometimes called a methadone clinic. You take your dose at the program at first. Once you are stable, you may be allowed to take some doses home. The naltrexone shot can be given in a medical office, but opioids must be fully out of your body first.

Cost: New York Medicaid covers all three. Most buprenorphine products and the naltrexone shot do not need prior approval from Medicaid. If you have no insurance or not enough coverage, the state's Buprenorphine Assistance Program (BUPE-AP) can pay for buprenorphine. Call 1-800-542-2437 to check if you qualify.
To start, ask your doctor, or call the NY HOPEline (1-877-846-7369, or text 467369) to find treatment near you. You can also search FindTreatment.gov.

entries.q: What is a peer advocate or recovery coach, and how do I find one?
a: A peer is someone who has lived through a similar struggle, like addiction or a mental health condition, and is trained to support others. Peers are not therapists. They use their own experience to listen, give hope, and help you find your way through services.

For addiction, New York has Certified Recovery Peer Advocates (CRPAs), sometimes called recovery coaches. They can help you get into treatment, support you after a hospital stay or jail, teach about different paths to recovery, go with you to medical appointments, connect you to recovery groups, and help you apply for benefits. They work in treatment programs, hospital emergency rooms, community programs and courts.

For mental health, New York Certified Peer Specialists are in recovery from a mental health condition themselves. Family Peer Advocates are parents or caregivers who have raised a child with emotional or behavioral needs, and they help other families. Youth Peer Advocates are young adults with lived experience who help young people.

To find one, ask your treatment program, clinic or hospital if they have peer staff. Recovery centers offer drug- and alcohol-free places for peer support, groups and activities. In Warren County, the Hope and Healing Recovery Community and Outreach Center is in Glens Falls. You can also search the OASAS support services list, call the HOPEline at 1-877-846-7369, or see the Substance Use and Recovery category in this directory.

entries.q: What is SPOA (Single Point of Access)?
a: SPOA (Single Point of Access) is the county process for referrals to high-intensity mental health services, such as intensive or supportive case management, residential (housing) programs, and Assertive Community Treatment (ACT) teams. The process is a little different in each county.

In Warren and Washington Counties, the Office of Community Services for Warren and Washington Counties runs SPOA. Adults must be over 18, have a serious mental illness, and need services because the illness makes it very hard to function in the community. Children and youth with a serious emotional disturbance have their own SPOA committee.
There, a referral needs the SPOA application, a signed release of information, and a psychosocial or psychiatric assessment. Residential programs need a few more forms.
For ACT, a referral can come from the person, a family member, a mental health agency, a hospital, police or a court.

In Saratoga County, SPOA is run by Saratoga County Mental Health. A provider or family fills out the adult or children's SPOA referral form from the county website and sends it with a signed release. Questions: call (518) 584-9030. Both SPOA offices are listed in this directory under Case Management.

entries.q: How does someone get OPWDD services (the Front Door)?
a: OPWDD (Office for People With Developmental Disabilities) serves people with developmental disabilities, such as intellectual disability. The disability must have started before age 22.

The "Front Door" is how OPWDD connects you to services. Step 1: call the OPWDD Infoline at 866-946-9733 and ask to be transferred to your local Front Door office. Step 2: OPWDD decides if you are eligible. Step 3: if you are, you start planning services with Front Door staff.

Eligibility usually needs a psychological report with IQ testing, an adaptive behavior assessment, a medical report and social evaluation from the past 12 months, and a history showing the disability began before age 22. A Care Coordination Organization (CCO) can help you through the process.
Being found eligible does not by itself give you most services. Many services also need Medicaid. If you are found not eligible, you may be able to ask for a fair hearing.

entries.q: What is the difference between Early Intervention and CPSE?
a: Early Intervention (EI) is for babies and toddlers under age 3 who have a disability or a developmental delay. It is run by the state Department of Health and your county. Services like speech, physical and occupational therapy can happen at home or child care. There is no cost to families.
To refer a child to EI, call your county Early Intervention program. The Growing Up Healthy Hotline, 1-800-522-5006, can give you the number.

CPSE (Committee on Preschool Special Education) is for children ages 3 to 5. It is part of your school district. If a child may need special education, a parent or professional can refer the child to the chairperson of the district's CPSE. The evaluation is at no cost to the family.

If your child is in EI, the EI service coordinator helps you plan the move to CPSE. The CPSE should decide eligibility by the child's third birthday so services can continue. Parents of eligible children can choose to move to preschool special education or stay in EI until the child ages out.

entries.q: Where can I get help for alcohol, drug or gambling problems?
a: Call or text the New York State HOPEline any time, 24 hours a day, 7 days a week. Call 1-877-846-7369 (1-877-8-HOPENY) or text HOPENY (467369).
The HOPEline is free and confidential. It helps with substance use and gambling problems, and services are available regardless of ability to pay.
For a mental health or suicide crisis, call or text 988, the 988 Suicide & Crisis Lifeline. It is free, confidential and open 24/7.

entries.q: My school-age child is struggling. What is the difference between an IEP and a 504 plan?
a: An IEP (Individualized Education Program) is a written plan for a student with a disability who needs special education. It sets goals and lists services, such as special classes or therapy. In New York, each school district's Committee on Special Education (CSE) decides who qualifies and writes the IEP for students ages 5 to 21. For younger children, see our entry on Early Intervention and CPSE.

A 504 plan comes from a federal civil rights law called Section 504. It covers students with a physical or mental impairment that substantially limits a major life activity, such as learning, reading or concentrating. The plan lists supports and changes (called accommodations) so the student can learn alongside other students. A student does not have to be failing to qualify. A different school team, not the CSE, handles 504 plans.

To ask for a special education evaluation, write a letter to the CSE chairperson or your child's principal. Say you think your child may have a disability and ask for an initial evaluation. Date it and keep a copy. The district must ask for your written consent. The evaluation is free and must be done within 60 calendar days after the district gets your consent.

Parents have rights. You get a copy of the evaluation report. If you disagree with it, you can ask for an independent evaluation (IEE) at the district's cost. You can also ask for free mediation or an impartial hearing. State-funded Family and Community Engagement (FACE) Centers help parents understand the process. A free legal aid office can help with your situation.

entries.q: Can my child go to Head Start or free pre-K?
a: Head Start is a free federal program that helps young children get ready for school. Early Head Start serves pregnant women and children from birth to age 3. Head Start preschool serves children ages 3 to 5. All programs welcome children with disabilities.

Who qualifies for Head Start: families with income below the federal poverty guidelines. Children also qualify no matter the income if they are in foster care, are homeless, or the family gets TANF (cash assistance), SSI or SNAP. Pregnant women may qualify for Early Head Start.

How to apply: contact your local program. Find it in the Pregnancy and Young Children category of this directory or with the Head Start Locator on headstart.gov. The program will check if your child qualifies, give you the forms, and tell you what papers to bring. If there is no space, ask to join the waiting list. For help finding a program, call 1-866-763-6481 (weekdays, noon to 6 p.m.).

Universal pre-K (UPK) is free pre-kindergarten through public school districts, sometimes held at child care centers. Any child who lives in the district can go the school year they turn 4 on or before December 1. There is no income test. Call your school district to ask when registration starts. If there are more children than seats, the district holds a lottery. Some districts also have pre-K for 3-year-olds.
Pre-K is growing. Under the 2026-27 state budget, every district can get state money for pre-K. By the 2028-29 school year, districts must offer pre-K to every eligible 4-year-old who applies.

entries.q: After someone is found eligible for OPWDD, what happens next?
a: After OPWDD finds someone eligible, Front Door staff give you information about the Care Coordination Organizations (CCOs) in your area. A CCO is an agency that provides a care manager. You choose the CCO, and the CCO helps you enroll.

You also choose a type of care management. Health Home Care Management is the full option. A care manager helps you get disability services and also coordinates medical, dental and mental health care, and links you to housing, jobs and family supports. Basic HCBS Plan Support is a very small option. It keeps your plan and paperwork up to date but does not coordinate health or mental health care.

Your care manager works with you to write your Life Plan. The Life Plan is built around your goals and needs. It covers your disability supports and your other services, like medical, dental and mental health care. It is reviewed regularly and updated when your needs change.

Most OPWDD services need Medicaid, including care coordination and HCBS waiver services (home and community-based services such as respite, day programs, supported employment and residential care). Front Door staff or a CCO can help you apply for Medicaid.

The CCO does not approve or cut services. OPWDD's regional office does that. If you are not happy, you can ask for a different care manager, change your level of care management, or switch to another CCO in your region.

entries.q: Who pays for rehab, home health care, a nursing home or assisted living?
a: Medicare pays for short-term skilled care, not long-term help with daily living. Skilled care is care from nurses or therapists, like wound care or physical therapy after a hospital stay. Help with bathing, dressing and eating is called custodial care, and Medicare does not pay for long-term care like that.

Rehab in a nursing home: after an inpatient hospital stay of at least 3 days, Original Medicare can pay for a skilled nursing facility (SNF) for up to 100 days in each benefit period, if you need daily skilled care. In 2026, you pay $0 for days 1 to 20 (after the Part A deductible, which you usually already paid for the hospital stay), $217 a day for days 21 to 100, and all costs after day 100. You usually must enter the SNF within 30 days of leaving the hospital. See the question on observation status.

Home health care: Medicare pays the full cost of part-time skilled nursing and therapy at home if you are homebound and a doctor or nurse practitioner confirms you need it. It does not pay for 24-hour care, meals, cleaning, or personal care when that is the only help you need.

Long-term care: Medicaid can pay for long-term care for people who qualify, at home (see the MLTC and CDPAP questions) or in a nursing home. Apply at your county Department of Social Services. Otherwise, people pay on their own or with private long-term care insurance.

Assisted living: Medicare does not pay for it. New York's Assisted Living Program (ALP) is for people who would otherwise need a nursing home but don't need constant nursing care. Both Medicaid members and people paying privately can use it. An ALP provides room, meals, personal care, nursing and therapy. Contact an ALP directly. For free help sorting out your options, call NY Connects or your county Office for the Aging (see the "Where do I start?" question).

entries.q: What does the Office for the Aging do, and who can use it?
a: Each county has an Office for the Aging. It helps people age 60 and older stay safe and independent at home. Many services, like meals, have no income limit. Some ask for a small voluntary donation, and in-home help uses a sliding scale (the cost depends on income).

Local offices: Warren County is served by the Warren/Hamilton Counties Office for the Aging in Lake George. Washington County has the Office for Aging and Disabilities Resources in Fort Edward. Saratoga County has its own Office for the Aging. NY Connects gives free, unbiased help with long-term care to older adults and to people of any age with a disability. Your county office can connect you, or call NY Connects statewide at 1-800-342-9871.

Home-delivered meals (often called Meals on Wheels) go to people 60 and older who are homebound and can't make their own meals. A spouse may get meals too. Group meals at senior dining sites are open to anyone 60 or older. A small donation is suggested but not required.

EISEP (Expanded In-home Services for the Elderly Program) gives non-medical help at home, like housekeeping, shopping, bathing and dressing, plus a case manager. It is for people 60 and older who need help with daily tasks and are not eligible for the same help through Medicaid. There may be a waiting list.

Offices also offer HIICAP Medicare counseling, caregiver support and respite (a break for caregivers), help with benefit applications, and rides for older adults. Call your county office to ask what is offered where you live.

entries.q: What is Adult Protective Services (APS), and what happens after a report?
a: Adult Protective Services (APS) helps adults age 18 and older who live in the community and, because of a physical or mental impairment, can't protect themselves from abuse, neglect or financial exploitation (someone misusing their money or property). It is for people who have no one willing and able to help them responsibly. APS is run by each county's Department of Social Services (DSS).

Anyone can make a report, and you can stay anonymous. Call your county DSS and ask for Adult Protective Services, or call the statewide line at 1-844-697-3505 on weekdays. If someone is in danger right now, call 911.

After a report, APS visits the person's home within three working days, or within 24 hours if the situation is life-threatening. A caseworker looks at the risks and offers help. Help can include counseling, medical or mental health checks, help applying for benefits, help managing money, homemaker services, or finding a safer place to live. In serious cases, APS can ask a court for protective orders or a guardian.

An adult who has mental capacity (can understand the risks and make their own choices) has the right to refuse help, even if others disagree. APS will keep offering help and try to convince the person to accept it. If there are questions about the person's capacity, APS will seek a mental health evaluation to decide if a court should step in.

entries.q: What is the difference between hospice and palliative care?
a: Palliative care is extra support for anyone with a serious illness, at any age and any stage. A team works to ease pain, other symptoms and stress. You can keep getting treatment to cure or control your illness at the same time. Anyone can ask for a palliative care referral.

Hospice is a type of palliative care for people near the end of life. For Medicare, your doctor and the hospice doctor must certify that you are expected to live 6 months or less if the illness runs its usual course. Care focuses on comfort instead of a cure. Hospice is usually given at home, or in a nursing home or assisted living. It also supports the family, including grief counseling for up to 13 months after a death.

Choosing hospice does not mean giving up all care. Medicare still covers health problems that are not related to the terminal illness. You can keep seeing your regular doctor. You can stop hospice and go back to treatment for your illness, and you can sign up for hospice again later.

Who pays: Medicare Part A covers hospice. You pay nothing for hospice care, except up to $5 per prescription for pain and symptom drugs and a small share for short inpatient respite stays. Medicare's hospice benefit does not pay room and board in a nursing home. New York Medicaid also covers hospice. Palliative care is billed in different ways, so ask a social worker or your health plan what is covered.

New York law requires doctors and nurse practitioners to offer information about palliative care and end-of-life options to patients expected to die within 6 months. You can always ask for it yourself. See the Hospice and Caregiver Support category in this directory.

entries.q: I'm a family caregiver and I need a break. What help is there?
a: Respite means short-term care for your loved one so you can rest, work, or take care of yourself. It can happen at home, when a worker comes in, or outside the home, such as at an adult day program, a senior center, or a short stay in a nursing home or assisted living.

Your county Office for the Aging runs caregiver programs. Through the National Family Caregiver Support Program, they can offer information, counseling, support groups, training and respite. You may qualify if you are an adult caring for someone 60 or older, or for someone of any age with Alzheimer's disease or a related dementia. Relatives 55 or older who are raising a child, or caring for an adult relative age 18 to 59 with a disability, may also qualify.
The State Respite Program and EISEP (in-home help for people 60 and older) can also provide respite. To ask, call your county Office for the Aging or NY Connects at 1-800-342-9871.

For memory loss or dementia, the Alzheimer's Association 24/7 Helpline is free: 1-800-272-3900. Staff can help with caregiver stress, behavior changes, safety, care planning, respite, and finding local programs. Interpreters are available in more than 200 languages.
If the person has Medicaid, CDPAP may pay a family member to give care (see our CDPAP entry). See the Hospice and Caregiver Support category in this directory for local help.

entries.q: I don't drive. How can I get around in Warren, Washington or Saratoga County?
a: If you have Medicaid, you can get free rides to medical appointments. See our entry on Medicaid rides. For other trips, here are the main options.

CDTA buses: CDTA (Capital District Transportation Authority) runs public buses in the Glens Falls area and in parts of Saratoga County. Glens Falls routes reach places like Hudson Falls, Fort Edward, South Glens Falls and Moreau. Routes and times change, so check cdta.org or call CDTA at (518) 482-8822.

Half fare: People 65 and older, people with a disability, and honorably discharged veterans can ride CDTA buses for half fare all day. You need a CDTA half-fare photo ID card. Bring a photo ID showing your age, or proof of disability such as a Medicare card, SSI or SSDI papers, or a VA disability letter.

STAR paratransit: STAR is CDTA's door-to-door ride for people whose disability keeps them from using the regular bus. It runs within 3/4 mile of CDTA bus routes, on the same days and hours. You must apply first, and your medical provider fills out part of the form. Book up to 7 days ahead, and no later than 4 p.m. the day before. A one-way trip currently costs $2.50.

Office for the Aging rides: Each county Office for the Aging has rides for people 60 and older, often for medical visits and errands. In Washington County, rides are arranged through LEAP, and eligible people 60 and older with no other way to travel can get free GoGoGrandparent rides (using Uber or Lyft). You must register with the Office for Aging first. Rural Washington County has very little public transit: CDTA buses there mainly serve the Hudson Falls and Fort Edward area. Plan ahead, and call 211 or see the Transportation category for more options.

entries.q: What is a health care proxy, and what is a MOLST?
a: A health care proxy is a form where you name a health care agent: a person you trust to make medical decisions for you if you can no longer make them. The state says everyone over 18 should have one. You can download the New York Health Care Proxy form from the Department of Health.
Talk with your agent about what matters to you. Give copies to your agent, your doctor and your family, and keep one in your wallet.

A MOLST (Medical Orders for Life-Sustaining Treatment) is different. It is a medical order form signed by a doctor, nurse practitioner or physician assistant, for people with serious health conditions. It records choices like whether to have CPR or a breathing tube.
In New York, the MOLST is the only approved form for a do-not-resuscitate (DNR) and do-not-intubate (DNI) order outside the hospital. It travels with the patient to other care settings.

entries.q: How do I get a New York State ID card?
a: Anyone of any age with lawful status in the U.S. can get a New York non-driver ID card. You must apply in person at a DMV office. You get a temporary paper document that day.

Bring a completed application (form MV-44), the fee, and proofs of identity. DMV uses a point system: your proofs of name must add up to at least 6 points, and you must show proof of your Social Security number, such as your card, or a letter saying you are not eligible for one.
If you are under 21, a parent or guardian can vouch for your identity by signing form MV-45 at the DMV and showing their own 6 points of proof.
Check the DMV's document list before you go, because some documents do not count for a REAL ID or Enhanced ID.
